config.theme: Incident postmortem: the checkout outage last Tuesday
config.author: claude-opus-5-5 (Claude Code session)

cast.theme: Incident postmortem: the checkout outage last Tuesday

personas.name: Nadia
personas.goals: Kill this class of incident for good
personas.hidden_agenda: Asked for cert automation budget a year ago and was told no

personas.name: Liam
personas.goals: Explain why it took so long to find
personas.hidden_agenda: Assumed it was a deploy and lost time chasing it

personas.name: Rosa
personas.hidden_agenda: Her VP is asking for a name to blame

personas.name: Kenji
personas.hidden_agenda: The expiring cert was on his team's spreadsheet

agenda.title: Root cause
agenda.goal: Understand why an expiring certificate went unnoticed

agenda.title: Customer and business impact
agenda.goal: Size the impact and settle refunds and comms

agenda.title: Follow-ups
agenda.goal: Owners and dates for the fixes

facts.statement: Checkout was down for 2 hours 10 minutes
Outage started at 9:40 am local time
The payment gateway certificate expired at 9:38 am
Certificate-expiry alerts fired in the last 90 days = 0
Time from start to identifying the cause = 74 minutes

beats.summary: When it started, when we knew; Liam undercounts the time to cause
Why nobody saw the expiry coming; the spreadsheet; Kenji's inventory number goes unchallenged
Orders, customers, money; Rosa's order number corrected; refunds misstated and corrected late

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Okay, thanks everyone. Blameless as always. Liam, take us through the morning?

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: So, checkout started failing at nine forty. Every payment call came back with a handshake error.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And when did we find out it was the certificate?

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: In hindsight, it felt like we found it in about half an hour.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Let's be precise. The incident log has seventy-four minutes from start to cause.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: Seventy-four. Yeah. We spent the first forty chasing the deploy from that morning.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Why the deploy?

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: There was a deploy at nine thirty. Two things changing ten minutes apart, you blame the deploy.

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: Technically, the cert expired at nine thirty-eight. Two minutes before the errors.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: So the deploy was a red herring.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: A very convincing one.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: From the customer's side, the app just said "something went wrong". No hint at all.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: How long were we down in total?

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: Two hours ten, start to finish. The renewal itself was fast once we knew.

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: Getting a new cert issued took about fifteen minutes. The rest was rollout.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Okay. So the timeline is clear. The gap is the seventy-four minutes to cause.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: In hindsight, the handshake error was the clue. I just didn't read it right.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Nobody's blaming you. Let's figure out why the system didn't tell you.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: Thanks.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Root cause. Kenji, how do we track certificate expiry today?

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: To be fair, it's a spreadsheet. Plus a calendar reminder for the big ones.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: A spreadsheet? For payment certificates?

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: For all of them. We have around two hundred certificates in the inventory.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And this one was in the spreadsheet?

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: It was. The reminder went to someone who left in the spring.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: So the alert existed, it just went to nobody.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Did any automated monitoring fire?

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: No. Zero cert-expiry alerts in the last ninety days. We never set them up for the gateway.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Look, my VP is going to ask whose fault this is.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Then the answer is "the process". A spreadsheet that depends on one person's calendar.

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: Technically, we renew about forty certs a year by hand. Something was always going to slip.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Forty a year, by hand?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And when was the last cert incident?

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: Fourteen months ago. The internal wiki, nobody really noticed.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: Fourteen months, and the lesson didn't stick.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Let's be precise about the fix. Should all certs auto-renew, or just the external ones?

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: To be fair, all of them, eventually.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: But the external ones first. The ones customers can hit.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Okay. External certificates move to automatic renewal first, internal ones after. That's the direction we're committing to.

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: Agreed.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Is automatic renewal something we can buy, or do we build it?

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: Buy, mostly. The cloud provider does it if the cert lives there.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: Did anyone else's coffee order fail on Tuesday, by the way? I couldn't even get a latte from our own app.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Mine did. I ended up at the gas station. Terrible coffee.

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: I made tea. Tea doesn't need TLS.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Okay, the impact. Rosa?

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: From the customer's side, about ten thousand orders failed. It was a disaster.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: The dashboard has sixty-two hundred failed orders. Ten thousand might be attempts, with retries.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Right, sixty-two hundred orders. From about forty-nine hundred customers.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And revenue?

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Finance estimates three hundred forty thousand. Some of those people ordered later, so it's softer than it sounds.

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: How many came back the same day?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: We gave delivery-fee refunds, right? Around twenty-five grand, I think.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Look, I'd like to do more than refund the delivery fee. These are people's groceries.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: What did you have in mind?

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: A credit. Ten dollars, maybe, for everyone affected.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Ten dollars times forty-nine hundred is real money.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: It's less than losing them.

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: Maybe we only give credits to people who didn't come back.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: That's harder to explain, though.

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: Sorry, that's my building's fire alarm test, it'll stop in a second.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: Sorry, I've got the refund report open. It's eighteen seven fifty in refunds, not twenty-five.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Eighteen seven fifty, okay.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Okay. We give a ten-dollar credit to every affected customer, plus the refunds already issued. Decided.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Thank you. I'll write the apology email and get it to legal by Thursday.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: It would be good if the email explained what actually happened, in plain words.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Follow-ups. Let's be precise: owner and date for each.

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: I'll move every external certificate to automatic renewal by the end of the month.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Thank you. And monitoring?

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: I'll add expiry alerts for every cert in the inventory, at thirty and seven days.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Every one of them, Liam. All three hundred and twelve.

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: Three hundred and twelve. I said two hundred earlier, that was wrong.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's fine. That's why we check.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: And error messages. Can the app say something better than "something went wrong"?

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: It can. It's a product decision what it says.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Then let's maybe look at that next quarter.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Someone should check the other payment providers' certs too, while we're at it.

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: Already on the list. To be fair, they're on the spreadsheet.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: The spreadsheet that caused this.

turns.speaker: Kenji
turns.text: The spreadsheet that is about to be retired.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Does my VP get a written summary, or do I just forward the notes?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Okay. Good review. Thank you, everyone.

turns.speaker: Rosa
turns.text: Thanks, all.
